A brand-new chat remembers nothing from an unrelated past chat. Only a Project — or content you paste in — carries context forward.
Chat is a single ephemeral conversation. A Project is a persistent workspace. Claude Code is agentic — it writes and runs things itself.

hall-of-memory.misconception: Every chat starts from nothing — Claude can never remember or persist anything.

mentorLessons.line: A Project is a self-contained workspace — its own chats, its own knowledge base — one home for everything a piece of work needs.
Set project instructions once and every chat inside that Project follows them — tone, role, rules — no repeating yourself.
Anything shelved in a Project's knowledge base serves every chat inside it — but chats don't read each other; only the shelf is shared.
Claude quietly distills your chat history into a synthesis of key insights — who you are, what you're working on — and carries it into new conversations.
Memory is yours to govern — view it, edit it, pause it, or reset it entirely from your settings.
An incognito chat leaves no trace — it is saved neither to memory nor to your chat history.
Each Project keeps its own separate memory space, so what Claude learns in one Project never bleeds into another.
When content is substantial and standalone — a document, code, a diagram, an interactive page — Claude sets it in its own dedicated window: an artifact.
Artifacts keep versions you can flip between, can be downloaded, and can be published so anyone with the link may use them — but once unpublished, that same artifact can't be published again.
Instructions shape how Claude behaves, knowledge is what it consults, memory is what it recalls about you, and artifacts are what it builds for you.

cowork-caverns.misconception: AI can't be delegated real work — you have to do everything yourself, step by step.

mentorLessons.line: Cowork is Claude's agentic workspace — the same engine that powers Claude Code, turned loose on knowledge work with no terminal required. You describe the outcome; it does the digging.
A remote session runs on Anthropic's servers in an isolated sandbox, not on your machine. Close the laptop, walk away — the work keeps going without you.
Claude only touches folders you've connected — never the whole drive. On desktop it reads and writes those files directly, no uploading and downloading by hand.
Don't hand-feed pebbles. State the outcome you want, and Cowork breaks the job into subtasks — even running parallel workstreams — and coordinates them itself.

Your tasks live in a list in the sidebar, and Claude reports the outcome — the finished spreadsheet, the memo — rather than narrating every swing of the pick. A push notification can fetch you when it's done or needs your go-ahead.
Cowork taps the same connectors, skills, and plugins as the rest of Claude. Connect your tools once and every dig can draw on them.
The ore that comes out is polished: Excel spreadsheets with working formulas, PowerPoint decks, formatted documents — real deliverables, not just chat text.

A scheduled task runs on its own cadence, remotely — your computer can be asleep and the shift still gets worked. Each run is its own session you can review, and you can pause, edit, or fire it on demand.
Be choosy about which tunnels you open. Keep credentials and financial records out of connected folders — a dedicated working folder is the safest shaft.
Projects group related tasks into workspaces with their own instructions, context, and memory — and what Claude learns in one project stays in that project.

mentorLessons.line: Claude in Chrome isn't another chat window — it's a browser extension. Claude reads, clicks, and navigates real websites alongside you, from a side panel right where you browse.

You choose the leash: ask-before-acting shows you a plan first; per-site permissions gate the rest. And some things — downloads, sensitive info, purchases — always come back to you.

Pick the right bridge. The browser agent works any site by using its actual pages; pair it with Cowork and Chrome gathers while Cowork builds the models and reports.

mentorLessons.line: MCP — the Model Context Protocol — is an open standard for connecting AI applications to external systems. Think of it as a USB-C port for AI: one standard plug, many devices.
A connector links Claude to an app you already use — it can retrieve your data and take actions inside that service. The silos were never sealed; they just lacked a bridge.
Three roles hold every bridge: the host (the AI application), which creates one client per connection, and the server, which provides the context. One dedicated client per server — no shared ropes.

A server offers three gifts: tools (functions the AI can invoke to act), resources (data that provides context), and prompts (reusable templates). Actions, information, and patterns — learn which is which.
A local server runs on your own machine and talks over stdio; a remote server runs elsewhere and talks over streamable HTTP, serving many clients at once. Same protocol, different roads.

Connectors typically use OAuth: you sign in to the service itself and grant specific permissions — no password handed over, and you can revoke it all by disconnecting. Claude never gets more access than you already have.

A custom connector reaches a server no one at Anthropic has verified. Only connect to servers you trust, read the permissions you grant, and disable tools you don't need — a malicious server can smuggle instructions through prompt injection.
Ready-made connectors live in the Connectors Directory; a custom one just needs its remote MCP server URL. Either way, you choose what gets bridged.

Cloud service? Use a remote connector — they work everywhere you use Claude. Local files, a localhost database, OS-level access? That needs a local desktop extension, which only works in Claude Desktop and Claude Code.

codeforge.misconception: Real developers do everything by hand — an agent in your codebase is a gimmick.

mentorLessons.line: Claude Code isn't a chat window — it's an agent at your anvil. It reads your codebase, edits files, and runs commands itself, working across many files to get things done.
Learn the rhythm of the forge: it finds the right files, shows you the proposed change, asks your approval, then strikes. You remain the master — it swings the hammer.
A CLAUDE.md at the project root is read at the start of every session. Write down what you'd otherwise re-explain — build commands, conventions, rules — and keep it specific and concise.
Permission modes set how often the agent pauses for your word. In plan mode it only reads and proposes — nothing touches your files until you approve the plan.
A slash commands the session itself: /clear for an empty context, /compact to summarize and free space, /permissions to set the rules, /resume to pick up an old thread.
When a side-quest would flood your main conversation with search results, send a subagent. It works in its own context window and returns only the summary.
Instructions shape behavior; hooks guarantee it. A hook is a shell command that always runs at a lifecycle point — format after every edit, or block a forbidden file before it's touched.
MCP connects the forge to the outside world — issue trackers, databases, design tools — so Claude acts on them directly instead of working from what you paste. But verify you trust each server first.
Speak git in plain words — 'commit my changes,' 'create a PR.' And when two tasks must run at once, give each session its own worktree so the edits never collide.

automation-spire.misconception: Without you watching, it all falls apart — nothing can run reliably on its own.

mentorLessons.line: A scheduled task fires on its own clock — hourly, daily, weekdays — and each firing starts a fresh session. Write the prompt as a complete standalone instruction, because the run remembers nothing.
Work scheduled to the cloud runs remotely — it keeps going while your laptop sleeps. Work bound to an open session stops the moment that session ends. Know which kind you built.
Wire Claude into GitHub Actions and a simple @claude mention in a PR or issue summons it — analyzing code, fixing bugs, opening pull requests, all following your project's CLAUDE.md standards.

A subagent works in its own context window and hands back only the summary. Delegate the noisy exploration; keep your main thread clean. Independent tasks can run as separate subagents simultaneously.
The Messages API is stateless: every request stands alone. If you want Claude to remember the conversation, your code sends the whole history back each time. That's not a flaw — it's your control.
Tool use is a contract: Claude never runs your function itself. It returns a structured request — this tool, these arguments — your code executes it and sends the result back. The loop is the power.

When every call carries the same heavy prefix — system prompt, big document, tool definitions — prompt caching lets Claude reread it from cache instead of reprocessing it. Stable content in front, changing content behind.

The Agent SDK is Claude Code's harness as a library — the tools, agent loop, and context management, programmable in Python and TypeScript. Raw API when you want a completion; Agent SDK when you want an agent that acts.

Match the automation to the trigger: a clock says scheduled task, a repository event says GitHub Actions, a big side-investigation says subagent, a custom product says the API or Agent SDK. The Spire has a floor for each.
